name: Hyaluronidase filler dissolving

lead: Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that cleave hyaluronic acid, the main ingredient of most popular dermal fillers. In aesthetics it is injected to dissolve filler that looks lumpy or bluish under thin skin, or to treat complications.
It has long been used in medicine to help other injected drugs spread. Registered trials found in the sources address eye surgery, anesthesia blocks and other uses, not filler dissolving.

paras: It breaks the bonds in hyaluronic acid, lowering viscosity and increasing tissue permeability. It does not act on non-HA fillers such as calcium hydroxyapatite.

Local reactions include pain, swelling and itching; systemic effects and rare hypersensitivity are reported (incidence about 0.05 to 0.69 percent per Grokipedia). Animal-derived and recombinant products differ in immunogenicity.

lead: Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that degrade hyaluronic acid (HA), a component of the extracellular matrix.[1] By lowering the viscosity of HA, it increases tissue permeability, which helps injected substances disperse.[2]

In cosmetic medicine it is injected to dissolve HA dermal fillers and to address filler complications.[2] Wikipedia calls it the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler.[2] Fillers not based on HA are not dissolved by it; a 2023 paper notes calcium hydroxyapatite filler cannot easily be dissolved.
Most published trials of hyaluronidase concern other uses such as eye surgery, nerve blocks and as a drug-spreading agent.[3]

paras: Established uses include ophthalmic surgery with local anesthetics, subcutaneous fluid absorption and subcutaneous urography.[2] Recombinant hyaluronidase is also combined with several biologic drugs, for example in the subcutaneous breast cancer product Phesgo.[4]
The enzyme is injected to dissolve HA filler, for instance when product appears lumpy or bluish beneath thin skin, or when complications such as vascular occlusion occur.[1][2]

Reported effects include injection-site pain, swelling and itching, plus rarely systemic reactions; Grokipedia cites hypersensitivity incidence of about 0.05 to 0.69 percent and pre-existing antibodies to recombinant PH20 in roughly 6 percent of people.[1] Dedicated hypersensitivity studies of ovine hyaluronidase (Vitrase) have been registered.[5]

Mammalian hyaluronidases cleave beta-1,4 bonds in HA, producing smaller fragments.[1] Degradation products of HA have been reported to be biologically active, including inducing angiogenesis in a 1985 study.[6]
Karl Meyer classified hyaluronidases in 1971.[2] Purified US products were approved in 2004 and 2005, ending with recombinant Hylenex.[2]

No studies found specific to dissolving cosmetic fillers among the sources reviewed. Registered trials cover other uses: Vitrase for vitreous hemorrhage (NCT00198510, n=750; NCT00198497, n=510), hypersensitivity to ovine hyaluronidase (NCT00198419, NCT00198458, n=65 each), as a spreading agent (NCT00198484, n=108), and as an additive to bupivacaine nerve blocks.[3][5][7]

timeline.event: Karl Meyer classifies hyaluronidases into three groups.[2]
Vitrase and Amphadase approved in the US.[2]
Hydase and recombinant Hylenex approved in the US.[2]
